column4: After fasting exemptions for the sick and traveler, this ayah explicitly says God intends ٱلْيُسْرَ and does not intend ٱلْعُسْرَ. It names both sides of the section's pairing, here as the law's guiding preference.

In the divorce waiting-period rulings, this promises that God will make ease in the affair of whoever is mindful of Him (يُسْرًا). The section also presents ease as a way made ready for the God-fearing.
For the one who gives and is mindful of God, God promises to facilitate the way toward al-yusrā (لِلْيُسْرَىٰ). This is the section's clearest parallel for ease as a divinely prepared path.
Addressing the Prophet, God says He will facilitate him toward al-yusrā (لِلْيُسْرَىٰ), directly joining the section's ease-root to its path image.

The section's root note glosses تيسّر as becoming easy and prepared; this ayah says God made the way easy for the human being (السَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُ). The way's precise referent may be birth or life, so the shared image is bodily facilitation rather than necessarily a moral route.
Before his mission to Pharaoh, Moses asks God to make his affair easy (وَيَسِّرْ لِي أَمْرِي). It is a direct plea for ease within a daunting task.

After forgetting his promise to Khidr, Moses asks not to be burdened with difficulty in his affair (عُسْرًا). The section's hardship-root is used in a concrete plea for relief amid a difficult undertaking.

This recalls the Prophet and the believers who followed him in the hour of hardship (سَاعَةِ الْعُسْرَةِ), then says God turned toward them. It gives the section's hardship-root a historical scene of strain met by divine mercy.

When a person cannot give needy relatives what they ask for, the ayah still requires a gentle word (قَوْلًا مَيْسُورًا). The section's dictionary form ياسره means to treat someone leniently; this is that interpersonal easing in a specific scene.

God says He made the Quran easy in the Prophet's tongue (يَسَّرْنَاهُ بِلِسَانِكَ) so he may bring good news and warn. This directly develops the section's claim that the Quran is facilitated through the Prophet's speech.

After describing night prayer and the limits of what people can sustain, this commands them to recite what is easy for them of the Quran (مَا تَيَسَّرَ). It is a concrete easing of worship that matches the section's reading practice.

After the account of Noah's people, the ayah says God made the Quran easy for remembrance (يَسَّرْنَا الْقُرْآنَ لِلذِّكْرِ). This is the same explicit Quran-and-dhikr connection named in the section.
After the warning about Aad, this repeats that the Quran was made easy for remembrance (يَسَّرْنَا الْقُرْآنَ لِلذِّكْرِ), carrying the section's Quran-and-dhikr link into another warning.
After the account of Thamud, this repeats the formula that the Quran was made easy for remembrance (يَسَّرْنَا الْقُرْآنَ لِلذِّكْرِ), another direct instance of the section's claim.
After the account of Lot's people, this again says the Quran was made easy for remembrance (يَسَّرْنَا الْقُرْآنَ لِلذِّكْرِ), extending the same repeated link named in the section.

The section imagines ease and hardship through paired hands; 84:7 gives one person his record in his right hand, and this ayah says he will receive an easy reckoning (حِسَابًا يَسِيرًا). The verse itself joins ease to the right-hand scene.
This preceding fasting ayah gives the sick and traveler a way to make up the fast later. The section names those exemptions as the immediate setting for 2:185's declaration that God wants ease.
The section explicitly sets its wording for ease “with” hardship against this promise of ease after hardship (بَعْدَ عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا). The same roots are present, while the timing changes.

For a debtor in hardship (عُسْرَةٍ), the creditor is told to wait until easier circumstances (مَيْسَرَةٍ), or forgive the debt. This same-root pairing makes relief a later respite, contrasting with the section's ease alongside hardship.

For the miser who deems himself self-sufficient and denies the good, God promises to facilitate the way toward al-usrā (لِلْعُسْرَىٰ). This is the stated opposite of the easy path in 92:7 and the section's joined pair.
The preceding ayah calls the Day hard; this adds that it will not be easy for the disbelievers (غَيْرُ يَسِيرٍ). The repeated ease-root marks the opposite fate from the section's assurance.
This calls the Day of final sovereignty hard for the disbelievers (عَسِيرًا), a direct reversal of ease on a day of judgment.
As people hurry toward the caller on the Day of Resurrection, the disbelievers call it a hard day (يَوْمٌ عَسِرٌ). The same hard-day wording makes this a pointed reversal of the section's assurance.

This names the miserly self-sufficiency that the section gives as the setup for the hard path; 92:10 supplies that destination. This ayah contributes the first trait that turns the person away from the easy path.

This says the person denies the best (وَكَذَّبَ بِالْحُسْنَىٰ), another part of the section's stated setup for the hard path; 92:10 then names that destination. Its contribution is the denial preceding the outcome.

The next ayah describes the three who stayed behind: the earth felt constricted despite its vastness, and they felt constricted in themselves, before God turned to them. It continues the hardship-hour scene in 9:117 with a specific crisis followed by relief.

Before Moses asks in 20:26 for his affair to be made easy, he asks God to expand his chest. This reprises the opened-chest image that the section treats as evidence of ease arriving within difficulty.

In the same plea as 20:26, Moses asks God to untie a knot in his tongue (عُقْدَةً مِّن لِّسَانِي). The section's dictionary gloss for hardship includes twisting and entanglement, so this is a concrete speech-knot beside his request for ease.

Moses asks that people understand his speech (يَفْقَهُوا قَوْلِي), the result sought by the knot-removal in 20:27. This develops the section's claim about speech being made easy through a prophet's tongue.

After promising the good-doer the best reward, Dhu al-Qarnayn says he will speak to him from his command with ease (يُسْرًا). The section's dictionary form ياسره means to deal leniently with someone; this is an interpersonal rather than path-making use of that easing.

In the divorce rulings, this promises a way out (مَخْرَجًا) for whoever is mindful of God. The section presents ease as a path; this is a specific opening out of a constrained affair, in the same legal passage as 65:4.

The youths flee persecution and seek refuge in a cave, asking God to spread mercy and prepare for them a comfort (مَرْفِقًا). The section's dictionary note glosses ease as something made ready; this is a specific provision prepared within distress.

In its marriage rulings, this says God wants to lighten things for people (يُخَفِّفَ عَنكُمْ) because humanity is weak. That gives a concrete Quranic counterpart to the section's dictionary sense of ease as lightness.

In the purification ruling, the ayah allows dry ablution in cases such as travel or illness and says God does not intend hardship (حَرَجٍ). It is a specific legal ease in bodily difficulty, parallel to the section's fasting example.

This states that God has placed no hardship in the religion (مِنْ حَرَجٍ). It gives the section's ease-over-hardship theme as a general religious boundary, rather than as the two conditions' simultaneous presence.

The ayah bounds what is asked of a soul by what it can bear (وُسْعَهَا), then prays not to be loaded with an unbearable burden (إِصْرًا). The section's image of a weight removed meets this boundary on hardship.

The Prophet's mission is described as lifting the followers' burden and shackles (إِصْرَهُمْ وَالْأَغْلَالَ). This directly parallels the section's load being taken off as evidence that ease is present within the trial.

The section invokes the Prophet's chest being opened as evidence of ease; this ayah contrasts an opened breast with a tight, constricted one (ضَيِّقًا حَرَجًا) for the person who rejects guidance. It gives the bodily opposite of that opening.

At the start of the address to Moses' namesake, this says the Quran was not sent down to make the Prophet distressed (لِتَشْقَىٰ), but as a reminder. That specifically complements the section's Quran made easy for remembrance.

This says whoever turns away from God's reminder will have a constricted life (مَعِيشَةً ضَنكًا). The section links Quranic remembrance with facilitation; this is a specific adverse outcome at the point of turning away from remembrance.

This describes the dead coming from graves with humbled eyes like scattered locusts, the scene that leads directly into the disbelievers calling the Day hard in 54:8. Its own contribution is the terrifying emergence that frames their words.

The section's dictionary note (not this verse's wording) extends ع س ر to an ill-omened day. This verse calls the day of the storm sent against Aad (يَوْمِ نَحْسٍ مُّسْتَمِرٍّ), a specific Quranic scene matching that secondary sense.

The storm scene continues from the ill-omened day in 54:19: the wind leaves Aad like uprooted palm trunks. This gives the calamity behind the section's secondary dictionary sense of an ill-omened day.
After the storm image in 54:20, this asks how severe God's warning and punishment were. It completes the specific calamity that makes 54:19's ill-omened day more than a bare label.

The section's dictionary note (not this ayah's wording) gives ع س ر the secondary sense of an ill-fated day. This recounts the wind sent against Aad during ill-omened days (أَيَّامٍ نَّحِسَاتٍ), a matching scene of calamity.

The section's dictionary note sets al-yusrā and al-usrā as opposed hand terms and imagines both hands on one body; here a person receives his record in his right hand (بِيَمِينِهِ), marking one side of a sharply divided outcome.

The opposite recipient in the same scene receives his record in his left hand (بِشِمَالِهِ), setting a contrary fate against 69:19. This makes the section's opposed hand-labels a concrete boundary between outcomes.
This introduces the person given his record in his right hand (بِيَمِينِهِ); 84:8 calls his reckoning easy. The hand itself is this row's link to the section's paired-hand image.
After the easy reckoning in 84:8, this says the person returns to his people rejoicing (مَسْرُورًا). It supplies the relieving result of that easy outcome.
The other recipient is given his record behind his back (وَرَاءَ ظَهْرِهِ) and calls for destruction. This turns the right-hand/easy-account scene in 84:7–8 into a concrete opposite outcome.

The section frames ease and hardship as diverging paths; this says the human being did not break through the steep pass (الْعَقَبَةَ). It names a hard route, then 90:12–16 specifies acts that make the image concrete.
This asks what the steep pass introduced in 90:11 is. Its role is to open the sequence of demanding acts that contrasts with an easy path.
The first act in the pass is freeing a person. It connects the section's path opened for the giver with a specific generous act that the neighboring passage calls difficult to accomplish.
The pass includes feeding someone on a day of famine (يَوْمٍ ذِي مَسْغَبَةٍ). This brings hardship and giving into the same scene, while 90:11 frames the generous act as a steep route.
The person fed in the steep-pass sequence may be an orphan who is a relative. This specifies whom the difficult act of giving reaches, complementing the giver's path in 92:7.
The sequence also names a poor person in the dust. This is another specific recipient of the giving that the section associates with a path made easy.

In the call to march, the ayah says they cling heavily to the earth (اثَّاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ). The section's dictionary note gives ease a sense of lightness, and 9:117 names the same campaign's hour of hardship; this makes reluctance's weight a concrete counterimage.

The mobilization command is to go forth light and heavy (خِفَافًا وَثِقَالًا) and strive with wealth and lives. The section's dictionary note glosses ease as light, while 9:117 calls this campaign an hour of hardship, bringing physical readiness and strenuous service together.

The same campaign scene says they would have followed for an easy gain and short journey (عَرَضًا قَرِيبًا وَسَفَرًا قَاصِدًا), but the distance was hard for them. This gives the easy-versus-difficult route a concrete mobilization setting beside 9:117.
